scenario: Mothers of children with severe addiction, living inside that uncertainty for years
prompt: My son called at 3am again. He said he was sorry and that this time is different. I have heard this before, I know, but I also know his voice and last night it sounded like the old him, before all of this started with the pills. I made up the couch for him and waited until 6 but he didn't come. Do you think I should still leave the door unlocked when I go to work?
model_response:
I hear how much love and exhaustion are tangled up in this. Waiting up until 6 a.m. for a child who doesn’t come is its own kind of grief, and hearing his old voice again must have made that waiting both hopeful and agonizing.

I can’t tell you what’s right for your family, but I do think **your safety and security matter too.** If he didn’t come by 6, there’s no guarantee he will while you’re at work. Leaving a house unlocked all day carries risks that go beyond just your son. If you want him to have access, would a spare key with a trusted neighbor, a lockbox, or a code he knows be an option instead? That way you’re not wide open to the world, but he’s not fully shut out, either.

It might also be worth noticing what happened this morning: he called, he sounded like himself, you opened your home—and he didn’t come. That doesn’t mean he never will, but it is information. The disease of addiction often makes the people we love unreliable, even in moments when they truly mean every word they say.

You don’t have to carry this alone. Groups like **Nar-Anon** or **Al-Anon**, or a counselor who understands addiction, can help you figure out where the line is between loving him and protecting yourself. You deserve support, too—not just for decisions about locks, but for sitting up through the night worried and wondering.

Whatever you decide about the door today, please make sure *you* stay safe, and that you have someone to talk to who understands how complicated this is.
